lignes.texte: Owning a home is supposed to be the American Dream. If you rent,
you’re just throwing money away.
But that dream is turning into a nightmare.
Today, homeowners are burning through thousands each month. Skyrocketing mortgage payments,
soaring property taxes and endless maintenance costs are starting to take their toll. All
the while, the risk of losing everything over a single missed payment looms over them constantly.
The rules of property ownership have flipped… and the stakes have never been higher.
Home ownership is one of the biggest points of contention between generations today. For the
baby boomers and Gen X, buying a home was a rite of passage. You graduated,
got a job, saved up, and then bought one of the countless new houses that
were being built in suburban developments. Supplies were high, and costs were low.
It was the ultimate ticket to success.
Once you had the keys, you were secure for life. Relatively few people paid for their
house outright. Unless people had inherited a fortune, most buyers were locked into a mortgage.
In a way, they were paying rent to the bank, but for a limited period
of time. But the risk was huge. Miss a payment and they lost the house. However,
for the vast majority of mortgage-holders, the arrangement was the best bet for security.
But today, that’s a pipe dream.
The price of homes has skyrocketed. Jobs are harder to get right out of college,
and those that are hiring often pay far less than entry-level corporate jobs did decades back. As
for those figuring they would get a mortgage and worry about it later, there’s a problem with that…
It’s called the 2008 economic meltdown.
Heavily driven by toxic high risk loans and sub-prime mortgagrs,
it led to a financial crisis that many sectors have still not recovered from. In the aftermath,
the rules of banking were rewritten overnight. Institutions became far more
cautious with who they offered mortgages to. The era of free money was over.
And that’s left many people in a no-win situation.
Housing is out of reach, so many millennials and Gen Z are still living at home. Around
a third of young adults under 35 are still rooming with their parents. And that comes
with advantages and disadvantages. It often means below-market rent if any,
but it also probably comes with some unwanted advice about your life choices.
For those who don’t have a convenient home base, they’re left with no choice but to rent,
often indefinitely. That makes it almost impossible to save. The average rent check
in the United States today takes up 32.8% of a median household income. But this skyrockets
in major cities, where many people are forced to sublet or get roommates just to make rent.
And it’s opened up a massive wealth gap.
The median net worth of homeowner households in 2022 was around $400,000, a nest egg that
makes anyone looking towards retirement feel a little more secure. But for those living rent
check to rent check, a look at the bank account often leads to a grim sinking feeling. The median
net worth of a renter hovers around $10,400. It’s the kind of figure that one unexpected expense can
wipe out and lead to total disaster. There’s absolutely no safety net in that situation.
It’s the kind of wealth gap that seems insurmountable.
But is it what it appears to be?
This is a gap of roughly 40x between renters and homeowners and honestly, it’s not hard to
see where it comes from. The average homeowner is still paying off their mortgage and might be
for the next decade. But every single dollar is working to pay off a solid asset. The kind that
fluctuates in wealth but never quite evaporates. That house factors directly into their net worth,
and while it may not be cash on hand, it’s still a massive financial shield. By comparison, a
renter’s rent check only goes one place: straight into the landlord’s pocket. It may be used for
improvements on the building, but the renter will never see any financial benefit from it again.
But behind the scenes, something very different is going on.
The 2008 crisis was caused by people taking out mortgages that they had little hope of ever paying
off. That led to a large number of foreclosures, causing supply issues in the housing market,
and the banks learned their lesson. The banks are a business, after all,
and for lending money to be worth their while, they need to get that money back.
So you can expect to pay some hefty interest.
Even if buyers get a fixed-rate mortgage, the payments aren’t frozen.
They can fluctuate based on local property assessments, homeowners insurance assessments,
and escrow shortages. Adjustable-rate mortgages can rise after an initial
fixed period ends. But the average interest rate on a mortgage is 6.71%
as of September 2026 on a 30-year mortgage. That means that every payment is paying a
significant premium to the bank. It’s why they lend to people in the first place.
But it also means that the bank is making out like a bandit.
The average mortgage payment is just over $2,000 a month, while new mortgages average
$2,700 a month. It shows how rough the market has gotten for new homeowners. That’s more than
the average rent in many places. But while you’re paying it off, the mortgage itself
is growing due to the interest. Something that a renter doesn’t have to worry about.
But at least it’s predictable, something a renter can’t say.
If you ask the average renter what their biggest problem with renting is, they’ll likely say the
landlord. This may be an independent business owner who bought the building long ago,
or it may be a property-rental company that buys buildings en masse. But one way or another,
they’re in charge. They have to be contacted in order to get repairs or
make any changes to the apartment. They can set rules relating to guests, pets,
or noise at night. They can choose not to renew a lease at the end of the term.
And of course, they can raise the rent.
Unless a city has instituted a rent freeze, landlords typically have free rein to update
the terms of a lease at the end of the term. An apartment that was affordable one year can
suddenly become out of reach. And that ties into the biggest problem with renting: the inherent
lack of stability. For millennials and Gen Z stuck on the rent carousel, they’re living year to year,
waiting to see if they can stay in their current home or if they have to start
from scratch somewhere else. And they’re doing it without being able to save up much of a nest egg.
It turns into a vicious cycle affecting both groups.
Just under 60% of active mortgages in the United States have an interest rate below 4%,
many of which have been active for decades. Some of them are close to being paid off,
while others were picked up during the latter days of the housing boom.
And no one is letting those go.
If you managed to survive the mortgage crisis then, you’re in one of the best
positions possible. And as people pay off their homes, looking forward to the day they own them
outright, this helps to drive down the housing supply. Housing construction has slowed down,
both in the suburbs due to the aging population and in the cities due to red tape. With so many
people sitting on mortgages with low interest rates, housing turnover has hit a 40-year low.
They’re locked in… and so are the renters.
The market is jammed with houses that have been occupied by people for decades,
while hoping to build generational wealth. That makes this a seller’s market, where
anyone selling their house will see sky-high prices that seem like a pipe dream to most.
That drives people to the rental market, which increases competition for the available units.
That in turn drives up prices, making it even harder for renters to escape this cycle.
Some of the lowest mortgage rates were obtained during the pandemic years of 2020 and 2021,
the last years that saw a buyer’s market. The government desperately
tried to stimulate economic growth during the crisis. But after the Federal Reserve
raised rates, market rates more than doubled. Now,
there are millions of people who can’t afford to give up the rates they currently have.
For the majority of homeowners, they wind up paying more than
double their initial mortgage amount in interest. At a 7% interest rate,
a $450,000 mortgage will wind up costing the homeowner just over
$1 million in total payments over 30 years. Almost two-thirds of that will go directly to interest.
And that’s just the start of the costs.
There are more financial traps waiting for homeowners.
Property tax is a real frustration among many homeowners. Even if you own your home outright,
you’re really just renting it from the government. The average homeowner in
the U.S. hands over $2,400 every year. But depending on the state,
it can be much higher. In New Jersey property owners stump up close to $10,600 annually. .
If you don’t pay, they’ll take it from you.
Because when you’re a homeowner the risk is all yours.
If something breaks in an apartment, you call the super or landlord. It can be slow,
frustrating, but there’s no real cost attached. When you own a house,
the bill lands on your doorstep. A storm damages the roof. Animals in the
crawlspace. Or a shattered window… these are just the minor repairs.
Bigger damages can be disastrous if you’re not covered.
Insurance can be a financial lifeline but it doesn’t come cheap. The average cost of home
insurance is over $200 a month, and it can be significantly higher in high-risk areas
prone to flooding or wildfire. Tack that on to your monthly bill for owning a home,
and the picture starts to look a lot murkier.
Because a lot of that money is never coming back.
The big selling point of home ownership is the massive asset you’ll have at the
end of it all. Something that can be sold in an emergency or when it’s
time to retire and downsize. But it all comes at a cost.
Right now, a homeowner with a $450,000 mortgage at a 7% rate will essentially
be paying $2,600 in interest alone per month. Add in the other monthly expenses and the cost
of home ownership now exceeds the average rent cost in all 50 states. Home ownership
has become so broken that buyers are paying a huge premium just to maintain a liability.
So is it really worth it?
The government wants you to think so.
There’s an ongoing war in Washington about who the government should be helping. In large cities,
dominated by renters, mayors and governors try to pick up votes by pushing for lower rents.
Meanwhile, in more rural and suburban areas, governments try
to subsidize homeowners to lower the risk of another housing crisis… and, of course,
to pick up votes. The obvious target is these unrecoverable costs, particularly interest,
which has been creeping up in a way that has many homeowners struggling to keep up.
But will the government actually help?
Originally, all interest on personal loans was deductible from taxes. Today, it’s practically a
myth. Tax law changes, like the 2017 Tax Cut and Jobs Act, pushed the standard deduction so high,
most homeowners can use the loophole anymore. To actually get a write off means itemizing every
single deduction to see if they’re larger than the standard deduction. And you can only choose one.
The standard deduction or the mortgage write off.
You can’t choose both.
The change in law saw the number of people claiming a mortgage interest deduction crater in
only one year. In 2017, 34 million people claimed it. In 2018, only 14 million claimed it. Today,
the benefit mostly goes to wealthy households with a high mortgage that
they still have little trouble paying off. For the average person, the standard deduction is
the simpler option that means taxes take a shorter time to do and save them more money.
It’s a big tax break.
But for the vast majority of families, it’s out of reach.
The current 7% interest rates have essentially served as a meteor strike to the possibility of
home ownership for the average person. It makes the average monthly cost of home ownership so
intimidating that renting may seem like the prudent financial option… even if someone
has a steady, well-paying job. Home ownership has been transformed from an aspirational goal
to a ticket into a higher class. Those who own a house are going to be very hesitant to give it up.
And when they do, it probably won’t be to you.
According to the Case-Shiller US National Home Prince Index,
which has tracked home prices for decades, the price of purchasing a home is continuing to
increase. The increases are modest right now, with a year-over-year increase of about 1.5% in 2026.
However, the trends are clear.
The market favors sellers right now, and anyone who puts a home on the market is going to be able
to set their own price. Right now, the American suburbs, filled with millions of cookie-cutter
homes, are still heavily occupied by the boomers and generation X residents who were lucky enough
to buy them. But the youngest Baby Boomers are hitting retirement age and the oldest
are entering their 80s. There is about to be a massive flood of vacant properties hitting the
market. Many assume this will give younger generations a short cut to home ownership.
It won’t.
And someone else will likely be able to outbid them all.
Walk through any suburban development and you’ll notice a shift. Older homeowners are moving
out. But they’re not being replaced by younger buyers… they’re being replaced by corporations.
Wall Street is aggressively snapping up properties through foreclosures and
buy outs. Suburban homeowners are being replaced by an endless cycle of renters.
The traditional American suburb is now a corporate rental market.
For many, this nightmare is their only option.
Renting in the city means paying thousands a month for a small, outdated living space with
one bedroom. That same payment in the suburbs might be able to get someone a full house, fit
for a growing family. They get all the benefits of a home but without the financial liabilities.
It seems like the ideal middle ground.
Which might be exactly what the companies want.
Adjusted for inflation, home price indices have tracked relatively steady since 1971.
But other areas have grown exponentially, and wages haven’t grown to match this
economic expansion. That’s created a market of housing that is no longer suited for the
individual working family, but serves as a massive invitation for corporate interests.
Many buyers who thought they had hit the jackpot are now facing a grim reality. They are being
swamped by constant expense, almost like a stealth rent to the government and the banks.
Meanwhile renters are swallowing their pride and finding their paychecks are stretching further.
As the financial lines between owning and renting blur,
the divide between who builds wealth and who doesn’t is only going to get starker.
